profile.purpose: Demonstrates Kenji's preferred method for boiling eggs so they peel easily (steaming fridge-cold eggs in an inch of already-boiling water, covered), with cook times for different doneness levels, and explains the Serious Eats and New York Times peeling tests behind it.
profile.thesis: No method is foolproof, but starting eggs in already-boiling water, rather than bringing them up from cold, makes by far the biggest difference to how easily they peel. Egg age barely matters for boiled eggs.
key_takeaways: Use an inch or so of already-boiling water in a lidded saucepan or wok. The eggs needn't be covered and can go in straight from the fridge.
Timing: about 3-4 minutes for soft, about 6 for medium/fudgy, 9 for hard with a golden yolk, 11-12 for a paler, chalkier yolk.
Starting in hot water lets the whites set before they fuse to the shell membrane. Starting cold makes them stick.
Blind tests with over 100 volunteers gave roughly an 80% clean-peel rate for the hot-start method, versus about 50-60% for other methods.
Egg age makes little difference to peeling, but fresher eggs help for fried and poached eggs.
Pricking the fat end with a thumbtack relieves air-space pressure in thin-shelled eggs and reduces the dent at that end.
Letting eggs cool naturally works slightly better than an ice bath; an ice bath is fine if you need them cold fast.
Baking eggs in a muffin tin makes them hard to peel and gives an odd baked flavor.
Peeling technique: crack both ends, then roll gently.

outline.title: Intro: no foolproof method
outline.summary: Kenji says no egg-boiling method is foolproof but claims his has the best results, backed by data.

outline.title: Setup: steaming eggs in a little boiling water
outline.summary: Water in a saucepan (or ideally a wok, so eggs can roll down the side), already boiling, fridge-cold eggs lowered in a single layer, then covered.

outline.title: Cook times for each doneness
outline.summary: Sets a 9-minute timer and gives times for hard, medium/fudgy and soft-boiled eggs.

outline.title: Origin story and Serious Eats tests
outline.summary: Recalls peeling 3-minute eggs as a restaurant line cook, then testing vinegar, salt, and cold versus hot starts with a staff panel at Serious Eats. The hot start was what mattered.

outline.title: New York Times blind peeling study
outline.summary: Describes repeating the tests with over 100 public volunteers peeling eggs blind. He measured subjective ease, flaws and peeling time, and reached the same conclusion with about 80% versus 50-60% success.

outline.title: Thin shells, cracking and the air space
outline.summary: Notes some brands have thicker shells, and explains pricking the fat end with a thumbtack to relieve air-space pressure and avoid cracks and dents.

outline.title: Egg age myth
outline.summary: A test of 60-day-old versus same-day eggs from a neighbor's hens showed no peeling difference. Age matters for fried and poached eggs because the membranes loosen.

outline.title: Cooling, heat level and the oven method
outline.summary: Prefers natural cooling over an ice bath, says to keep a heavy simmer or light boil without letting the water evaporate, and dismisses muffin-tin baked eggs.

outline.title: Peeling demo and cut egg
outline.summary: Peels an egg by cracking both ends and rolling, then halves it to show a 9-minute yolk.

outline.title: Outro
outline.summary: Plans egg salad sandwiches for lunch and signs off.
